studies.tldr: Narrative review (2018): Z0011, IBCSG 23-01 and AMAROS support ALND omission in T1-T2 cN0 pts with low-volume SLN disease undergoing BCS + WBRT.
details: 🔍 Narrative review, Oncology (Williston Park) 2018; ALND vs axillary RT after positive SLNB, plus RNI/PMRT decisions

studies.significance: For RT, the transferable detail is the field. Z0011 omission rests on WBRT, with incidental axillary dose credited by the authors, while AMAROS required undissected axilla plus supraclavicular fields. ASCO 2016 conditions ALND omission on conventionally fractionated WBRT, so hypofractionated or tangent-only technique falls outside the guideline as quoted.
studies.monday_clinic: In T1-T2 (≤5 cm) cN0 pts with 1-2 positive SLNs having BCS and conventionally fractionated WBRT, this supports omitting completion ALND; it does not extend to tumors >5 cm or gross extranodal extension, which the trials did not enroll.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Narrative review by two authors (2018), drawing on published trials and current guidelines. **Not a systematic review**; no pooled estimate.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Built on **ACOSOG Z0011** (N=891; 10-yr LRR **6.2% vs 5.3%, P = .36**), **IBCSG 23-01** (N=931, N1mi) and **AMAROS** (axillary + supraclavicular RT vs ALND). NSABP B-04 is cited as the biological precedent: about 40% predicted axillary disease, only 20% regional recurrence.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents T1-T2 cN0 breast cancer with 1-2 positive SLNs or micrometastases treated with BCS and WBRT. Does not represent tumors >5 cm, gross extranodal extension, or (in this excerpt) mastectomy and post-NACT pts.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The authors hold that **omission of ALND is now standard** for low-volume nodal disease after BCS. Z0011's result may partly reflect **incidental axillary irradiation**, which makes RT field design part of the surgical de-escalation decision.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Published 2018, so later axillary de-escalation data are not covered. The excerpt cuts off before the mastectomy, PMRT and NACT sections, so those recommendations cannot be checked against the source.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The field drives the decision: Z0011 used WBRT, with possible incidental axillary dose, while AMAROS deliberately treated the undissected axilla plus supraclavicular region. ASCO 2016 ties ALND omission to conventionally fractionated WBRT, so changing technique or fractionation moves outside the population the guideline rests on.
significance_by_specialty.surgonc: Completion ALND after 1-2 positive SLNs in BCS pts found more involved nodes in <40% historically, and Z0011 showed 10-yr LRR 6.2% vs 5.3% (P = .36) without it. Omission is less certain for tumors >5 cm or gross extranodal extension, which these trials excluded.

studies.tldr: RNI raised DFS in MA.20 (82% vs 77%) and EORTC 22922 (72.1% vs 69.1%), neither showing OS gain; 2017 patient-selection review.
details: 🔍 Narrative review (The Breast 2017); no new data, no systematic search described

IMC coverage for node-negative medial tumors rests on 22922; full nodal fields in low-volume pN1 rest on MA.20.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Narrative review by MD Anderson radiation oncologists (The Breast, 2017). **No systematic search or pooled analysis** stated; no grant funding, no conflicts declared.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **MA.20**: IMC (first 3 intercostal spaces) + SCV + undissected axilla after BCS. **EORTC 22922**: IMC + medial SCV after BCS or mastectomy. A technique figure contrasts standard tangents, high tangents (level I/II axilla), and deep-tangent or electron IMC fields.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Built on NCIC MA.20 and EORTC 22922 for intermediate-risk disease, with ACOSOG Z0011 and AMAROS framing axillary surgery. Neither RNI trial showed OS benefit alone; adding a French IMC trial, a meta-analysis gives an **absolute 1-2% 10-yr OS** gain.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents stage II-III breast cancer, node-positive or high-risk node-negative, after BCS or mastectomy. Does not represent nodal pCR after neoadjuvant chemotherapy, which the authors defer to NSABP-B51.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Cardiac toxicity estimates come from a 1958-2001 cohort and a retrospective IMC series, both predating CT-era planning. Subtype and Oncotype modifiers in the algorithm are **not prospectively validated** for RNI.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Authors favor a continuous risk spectrum over a node-count threshold: grade, subtype, nodal burden and extent of axillary surgery guide RNI in stage I-II. SLN upstaging makes modern pN1 lower-risk than the trial cohorts, which likely **shrinks the absolute benefit**.

studies.interpretation:
The review is most useful now for how it frames the selection problem, not for settling it. Its core evidence is two randomised trials that asked overlapping but distinct questions. NCIC MA.20 was almost entirely a BCS, chemotherapy-treated population with 1-3 positive nodes, treated with a wide field that added the level III axilla to IMC and SCV. EORTC 22922 enrolled a broader mix, including mastectomy pts and a large node-negative fraction selected for central or medial tumors, and treated only IMC plus medial SCV. Pooling them under one label, RNI, blurs a target-volume question into a population question. 22922 is the better evidence for IMC coverage in node-negative medial disease, and MA.20 for full nodal fields in low-volume pN1 after dissection. A reader deciding whether to add IMC for a lateral tumor with one positive node is extrapolating from both.

The effect sizes are modest and consistent: a few absolute points of DFS, a breast cancer mortality reduction in 22922, no OS gain in either trial alone, and a pooled absolute OS difference of 1-2% only once a French IMC trial is added. A benefit of that size can be erased by toxicity, which is why the authors pair it with the cardiac dose-response data and the IMC coronary disease series. Both carry era problems: the dose-response cohort was treated from 1958 to 2001, and the IMC series is retrospective. Modern CT-planned IMC coverage probably costs less cardiac dose than those data imply, but the review offers no contemporary dosimetry to show it.

The more durable argument is about denominators. Sentinel node microsectioning and IHC turn a sizable share of previously negative nodes positive, so a modern pN1 cohort is more favorable than the pN1 pts in either trial, and the absolute RNI benefit should shrink with it. ACOSOG Z0011 sharpens this. It reads as evidence that SLN-positive pts can skip ALND, but roughly half of the pts with RT records had high tangents and about a fifth had dedicated nodal fields, so the no-dissection arm was partly an RT arm. AMAROS gives the cleaner contrast, axillary RT against ALND, with low axillary recurrence in both arms, though it was underpowered for non-inferiority.

The review is weakest where it moves from these trials to its risk-spectrum algorithm. The proposed modifiers (lymph node ratio, age, grade, LVI, extracapsular extension, subtype, Oncotype) come from retrospective prognostic work, and the authors concede the Oncotype-RNI link has not been tested prospectively. The subtype point rests on a Danish Breast Cancer Cooperative Group 82b/82c tissue analysis that placed the PMRT OS benefit in ER/PR-positive, HER2-negative disease. That runs against the instinct to reserve RNI for TNBC, but it is a post-hoc biomarker read and should be weighted as one.

The post-neoadjuvant section was written while Alliance A011202 and NSABP-B51 were still accruing, so its guidance there points to trials rather than to evidence. Read the paper as a well-organised map of the question as it stood in 2017, and check the later readouts before applying its post-NAC recommendations at a tumor board.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The two trials irradiated different volumes: MA.20 added level III axilla to IMC + SCV in a cohort with 84.9% having 1-3 positive nodes, while 22922 treated IMC + medial SCV only, with 44.4% node-negative. IMC coverage for node-negative medial tumors rests on 22922; full nodal fields in low-volume pN1 rest on MA.20.
significance_by_specialty.surgonc: Z0011's SLND-alone arm was partly irradiated: ~50% of 228 pts with RT records had high tangents, 19% nodal fields. AMAROS axillary RT vs ALND gave 5-yr axillary recurrence 1.19% vs 0.43% with less lymphedema, framing RNI as the ALND alternative for SLN-positive early disease.

studies.name: Radiation decisions after neoadjuvant chemotherapy and mastectomy
studies.tldr: Retrospective MDA and NSABP data: PMRT after NACT and mastectomy cuts LRR in cT3-T4, cN2-N3 and ypN+ disease; omission after ypN0 has no randomised test.
details: 🔍 Personal View (Lancet Oncol 2012): no randomised PMRT data exist after NACT and mastectomy
🔍 Evidence base: retrospective MD Anderson series plus NSABP B-18/B-27 mastectomy pts, in whom RT was prohibited
📊 NSABP B-18/B-27 without PMRT: 8-yr LRF 14.9% if ypN+ (n=447) vs 5.9% with pCR and ypN0 (n=68)

details.text: 📊 MDA 10-yr LRR with vs without PMRT by subgroup (n=676, 80% irradiated, median f/u 69 mo)

rows: Four or more nodes at resection

details.text: ⚠️ cT3N0 after NACT: the series disagree on PMRT need
subdetails: MDA (n=162): 5-yr LRR 24% without vs 4% with PMRT (p<0.001)
NSABP no-PMRT 10-yr LRF: 14.0% ypN+ (n=179), 11.8% ypN0 with residual breast disease (n=95), 6.2% ypN0 with breast pCR (n=16)

details.text: ⚠️ Good responders: pCR / ypN0 series conflict for clinical stage III

details: 📐 Le Scodan ypN0 overall: adjusted HR 0.37 (95% CI 0.09-1.61), p=0.18 for PMRT
📊 Age <35, cStage IIA-IIIC (MDA, n=107): 5-yr LRR 37% without vs 12% with PMRT (p=0.001)
📊 Same cohort: 5-yr OS 48% without vs 67% with PMRT (p=0.031)
🔗 NACT shifts risk: four or more nodes at surgery, 5-yr LRR 53% after NACT vs 23% after upfront surgery
⚠️ MDA pts recur across several publications; concordance between MDA series is partly double-counting
⚠️ Era effects in staging, imaging, chemo and surgery across cohorts treated 1974 to 2005
🔍 Authors' MDA practice: PMRT for cStage III, cT3 and most ypN+; selective in cStage II (young, ER-negative, poor response)
studies.significance: The unresolved zone is cT3N0 converting to ypN0: MDA shows 5-yr LRR 14% vs 2% with PMRT (p=0.06), while NSABP no-RT cohorts report 6.2% after breast pCR, so omission there depends on which cohort you trust. Same split for cStage III pCR: MDA 33% vs 7.3%, Le Scodan no benefit.
studies.monday_clinic: In cT3-T4, cN2-N3 or ypN+ disease after NACT and mastectomy, this synthesis supports PMRT on clinical-stage risk; in cT1-T2 ypN0 it frames omission as a reasonable discussion on <10% LRR, not a randomised standard.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Personal View (narrative review), Lancet Oncol 2012. Medline/Embase search through **October 2011**, inflammatory breast cancer excluded. Evidence is **retrospective MD Anderson series** plus NSABP B-18/B-27 mastectomy pts with RT prohibited.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Non-metastatic, non-inflammatory breast cancer after mostly doxorubicin-based NACT and mastectomy. NSABP pts were earlier stage: only **43%** had clinical tumour >5 cm and **35%** clinical node involvement.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Threshold read: LRR of **at least 15%** without PMRT in ypN+ disease supports PMRT; LRR **<10%** in cT1-T2 ypN0 supports omission. Conflict persists for **cT3N0 ypN0** and **cStage III pCR**.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Danish and Canadian randomised trials and the EBCTCG meta-analysis set PMRT indications after **upfront** mastectomy; in EBCTCG node-positive pts, PMRT cut 5-yr isolated LRR 22.8% vs 5.8%. None of these enrolled NACT pts, so post-NACT pathologic stage does not map onto those indications.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents pts with non-inflammatory, non-metastatic breast cancer treated with NACT and mastectomy. Does not represent pts after breast-conserving surgery or with inflammatory breast cancer.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Cohorts are mostly doxorubicin-based, treated 1974 to 2005. Nodal conversion can reach **74%** with trastuzumab-based NACT, so today's ypN0 group may differ from the one these series describe.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Clinical stage before NACT and pathologic response both set LRR risk, so **documenting nodal basins before chemo** (US plus FNA of suspicious nodes) is a prerequisite for the PMRT decision. Omission after nodal conversion stays open, with RAPCHEM (non-randomised) and a proposed Alliance randomised trial placed to answer it.

studies.interpretation:
The argument here is structural rather than statistical. Every PMRT indication the field trusts came from trials that staged pts pathologically after upfront surgery, and NACT breaks that staging: it modifies pathologic extent in 80-90% of pts, so a ypN0 axilla after chemotherapy is not the same risk object as a pN0 axilla at upfront mastectomy. The MD Anderson comparison makes that concrete, with residual disease after NACT carrying higher LRR across pathologic tumour sizes than the same size found at upfront surgery. A reader who applies upfront-surgery rules to ypT/ypN alone will undertreat, and the authors' answer is to anchor on the worse of clinical and pathologic stage.

Where that anchoring is safe, the two evidence streams agree. cT3-T4, cN2-N3 and ypN+ disease carry LRR without PMRT that most radiation oncologists would treat, and the MDA series show large absolute reductions with PMRT in those groups. These estimates come from non-randomised comparisons, but in several series the irradiated pts carried more adverse features, which should blunt rather than inflate the apparent RT effect. That supports the direction, not the magnitudes.

The interesting zone is where the streams disagree, and it is the zone NACT keeps enlarging. For cT3N0 the MDA data favor PMRT even after ypN0, while NSABP B-18/B-27 no-RT cohorts show failure rates low enough that omission after pCR looks defensible. For cStage III with pCR, MDA reports benefit against an unirradiated group of 12 pts, while the Le Scodan series finds none. The discrepancy is plausibly selection: the MDA retrospective cohorts were more advanced than NSABP trial pts, and a prospectively followed trial cohort records failures differently from a chart review. Small unirradiated denominators do the rest; an LRR estimate built on 12 pts should not move a decision in either direction.

Three limits deserve weight. MDA pts recur across publications, so agreement among MDA series is partly the same pts counted again. The cohorts predate modern systemic therapy, and the authors note nodal conversion up to 74% with trastuzumab-based NACT, which changes who sits in the ypN0 group. And the 15% and 10% thresholds framing the conclusions are clinical conventions, not outcomes shown to track survival after NACT; the Danish reanalysis the authors cite suggests survival gains at 5-yr LRR risk as low as 11% after upfront surgery, which, if it transfers, argues for a lower bar than 15%.

The durable contribution is the frame: decide PMRT after NACT on pre-chemo clinical stage plus nodal response, document the nodal basins before chemotherapy so that decision is possible, and treat omission after nodal conversion as a randomised question rather than settled practice. The authors position RAPCHEM and a proposed Alliance randomised trial as the studies that would close it.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The unresolved zone is cT3N0 converting to ypN0: MDA shows 5-yr LRR 14% vs 2% with PMRT (p=0.06), while NSABP no-RT cohorts report 6.2% after breast pCR. Same split for cStage III pCR: MDA 33% vs 7.3%, Le Scodan no benefit.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Narrative **review** in Lancet Oncol (2022). PubMed MeSH search 1995 to April 2022 plus authors' files, English only; references chosen for originality and relevance, no formal synthesis.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Core argument is **urethral steering or sparing**: limit hotspots (steering) or dose below prescription (sparing) using IDC or MRI urethral delineation. FLAME-derived constraint: **urethra D0.1 cm³ <105%** of prostate prescription; SBRT systematic review supports **Dmax <107%** at 40 Gy in five fx.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Late toxicity can appear decades out and is often intractable. ASCENDE-RT brachy boost carried **18.4% vs 5.2%** stricture; anticoagulation raised 4-yr G3+ bleeding to **15.5% vs 3.6%**; second-malignancy absolute increase 0.1% to 3.8%.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: FLAME showed DIL boosting improves bDFS (**HR 0.45**) without mandating urethral limits, with GU toxicity 28% vs 23%. The randomised SBRT trials that would test urethral steering prospectively (NINJA, PACE-B, HEAT, NRG GU005) are listed as ongoing or closed to accrual.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The authors frame cure vs urinary morbidity as a balance improvable by **dose redistribution**: boost the MRI-dominant nodule, spare the urethra. The underdosing risk is accepted only when tumour localisation by MRI and/or PSMA PET is reliable and disease sits away from the urethra.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Urethral dose-toxicity evidence is largely retrospective and physician-reported with blunt scales, so no validated threshold exists. TURP effect on toxicity is drawn from heterogeneous series with no quantitative synthesis possible.

studies.interpretation:
The useful contribution of this review is that it reframes urinary toxicity as a planning problem rather than an unavoidable tax on dose escalation. The traditional picture, illustrated by ASCENDE-RT, is that more dose buys more cure at the cost of more strictures. The authors argue that the trade-off is partly an artefact of where the dose goes, and that the urethra, which carries much of the late morbidity, can be steered around without giving back tumour control.

The strongest support comes indirectly from FLAME. That trial boosted the dominant intraprostatic lesion with no urethral constraint, improved bDFS with HR 0.45, and still produced only a modest rise in moderate-to-severe GU toxicity, 28% vs 23%. Because the urethra was unconstrained, the investigators could look back at dose to urethra and bladder and find a dose-effect relationship, which is where the D0.1 cm³ below 105% recommendation comes from. Readers should hold that constraint lightly: it is a post hoc dosimetric association with no clear threshold, not a randomised comparison of constrained and unconstrained plans.

The ultrahypofractionation data make the same point more sharply. The MSKCC escalation to 40 Gy in five fractions without urethral sparing reported late moderate-to-severe GU toxicity of 34.3%, while the systematic review of 23 prospective trials estimated 7.7% when urethral Dmax stayed below 107% at the same prescription. That contrast is the most actionable number in the piece for anyone escalating SBRT dose, but it compares an observed phase 1 cohort with a modelled expectation across heterogeneous trials, so the true gap is uncertain. The tension the authors name honestly is underdosing: sparing the urethra risks missing periurethral disease, and they confine sparing to pts whose tumour is well localised on MRI or PSMA PET. The four sparing trials in the review showed no relapse signal, but those are small series, and relapse is a late endpoint.

The brachytherapy section is the weakest ground. Eleven different urethral constraints in the ABS HDR guidance is a sign that the field has no validated one, and the authors concede that most dose-point data are retrospective and physician-graded. Their measurement critique matters beyond this review: CTCAE, RTOG grading and IPSS under-capture chronic urgency, so series reporting low late GU toxicity may be measuring the wrong thing.

What the review cannot settle is whether urethral steering preserves control at scale. That answer sits with NINJA, PACE-B, HEAT and NRG GU005, none reported here. Until then, the practical takeaways are dosimetric caution at the urethra when boosting or escalating SBRT, early salvage over adjuvant RT post-RP, and active risk management for pts on anticoagulants or with prior TURP.

studies.name: SBRT in the management of liver metastases
studies.tldr: BED >100 Gy10 linked to 3-yr LC 93% vs 65%; review maps liver-met SBRT fractionation to OAR distance and liver/luminal constraints.
details: 🔍 Narrative review, Semin Radiat Oncol 2023; evidence summarized is prospective phase I/II series plus retrospective databases
📊 427-pt CyberKnife database: 2-yr LC 72%, 2-yr OS 49%, no G3+ toxicity
📊 CRC liver-met meta-analysis (656 pts): 2-yr LC 59%, 2-yr OS 57%
⚠️ G3+ liver toxicity 8.7% in that CRC meta-analysis
📐 BED >100 Gy10 in metastases: 3-yr LC 93% vs 65%
📊 Metastases vs primary liver tumors: 3-yr LC 76% vs 86%
📊 Single-fraction 35-40 Gy (BED 157.5-200 Gy10), median size 2.0 cm: 4-yr LC 96.6%

details.text: 🔍 Suggested dose/fractionation by distance to OAR (non-cirrhotic liver)

rows: <1 cm from luminal GI or central biliary tree

details: 📐 HyTEC (12 studies): ≥700cc liver <15-17 Gy as planning rule → G3+ toxicity 9.3%
📐 QUANTEC: MLD 15 Gy/3 fx or 20 Gy/6 fx → G3 liver enzyme risk <20%
🔗 SBRT vs RFA meta-analysis (2238 pts): 2-yr LC 84% vs 60% in liver-met studies
⚠️ No OS difference vs RFA despite the LC gain
⚠️ Liver constraints derive from conservative trial experience, not tolerance-defining dose escalation
⚠️ CRC radioresistance contested: some series show no histology gap at high dose
⚠️ Prognostic scores (Kress: median survival 34.4 to 2.8 mo, score 0 to 3) lack external validation
studies.significance: Being near bowel or the central biliary tree does not mean giving up ablative intent: the review moves tumors <1 cm from luminal GI or central biliary tree to 60-67.5 Gy in 10-15 fx, and uses SIB for the 1-2 cm zone. Pair that with the BED >100 Gy10 target and luminal organs, not the liver, set the fractionation.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Narrative review of liver-metastasis SBRT covering prospective series, pooled analyses, dose/fractionation, OAR tolerance and motion management. **Not systematic**; no new data.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: 1-6 fractions used, **3-5 most common**. **BED ≥100 Gy10** to PTV when LC is the priority; protract to **10-15 fx** for tumors <1 cm from luminal GI or central biliary tree. Caution in the **central liver zone** (2 cm shell around the portal vein).

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: HyTEC: GI toxicity tracked **prescription dose**; G3+ liver enzyme rise was not related to MLD. In 6-fx SBRT, G3 liver enzyme risk was **0% at MLD ≤15 Gy** but 6-18% at MLD ≤21 Gy depending on D800cc. QOL dipped after treatment and recovered **by 12 weeks** in a 60-pt prospective cohort.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Against RFA, a 2238-pt meta-analysis found **2-yr LC 84% vs 60%** for SBRT with **no OS difference** and G3+ toxicity <5% for both. HyTEC and QUANTEC supply the liver dose metrics; the ASTRO liver-primary guideline supplies the MLD and 700cc limits.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents non-cirrhotic pts with liver oligometastases evaluated for ablative SBRT. Does not represent cirrhotic livers or HCC, where limits are tighter.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Table 2 pools heterogeneous series from 2001-2018 with mixed histologies, platforms and dose ranges. The OAR-distance fractionation ladder rests on reviews and a pancreatic SIB paper, not on liver-met trials.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The practical output is a planning hierarchy: **luminal GI first**, then central biliary tree, chest wall and liver. The LC advantage over RFA has not shown up as an OS difference, which leaves patient selection, still subjective, as the step that matters most.

studies.interpretation:
The review's most useful contribution is turning a scattered phase I/II literature into planning logic. The dose-response argument rests on a pooled analysis rather than a randomized comparison: metastases appear less radiosensitive than primary liver tumors, and crossing a BED of 100 Gy10 tracks with 3-year LC of 93% versus 65%. That is a cross-study association. It is confounded by tumor size, motion management and treatment era, all of which the authors themselves list as predictors of LC. Read the 100 Gy10 threshold as a planning target with plausible biology behind it, not as a validated cutoff.

The fractionation ladder keyed to OAR distance is where the piece is most useful to a practicing radiation oncologist. Many clinics treat this as a binary choice between ablative 3-fraction SBRT and a palliative dose. The review argues instead that stretching treatment to 10-15 fractions keeps ablative intent next to bowel or the central biliary tree, with an SIB as a bridge for the 1-2 cm zone. That is expert synthesis built on institutional experience. The cited support is largely reviews and a pancreatic SIB paper, so the doses are defensible practice but not regimens tested in liver metastases specifically.

The comparative evidence is thinner than the favorable framing of SBRT suggests. The SBRT-versus-RFA meta-analysis shows an LC advantage with no OS difference. Its pooled studies were not randomized, so lesion size and location probably steered pts toward one modality or the other. LC without survival separation is the expected pattern when systemic progression drives outcome, which is why prognostic scoring matters. But the scores cited are retrospective and unvalidated, and selection remains the subjective step the authors concede it is.

On toxicity, the review is honest that liver constraints come from conservative trial experience, not from studies designed to find tolerance. Because dose-volume reporting was inconsistent, HyTEC could relate toxicity only to mean liver dose and prescription dose. The GI toxicity signal followed prescription dose, not liver metrics. That supports the review's own ranking, with luminal organs first. The 6-fraction data, where toxicity at a similar MLD varied with D800cc, show that MLD alone can mislead.

Only randomized data would change this read. The reference list includes MAESTRO, a randomized phase II of MR-guided adaptive versus ITV-based SBRT, and a phase 3 trial of single-dose versus 3-fraction SBRT in oligometastatic disease. The review reports no liver outcomes from either, so neither yet settles the technique or fractionation question here.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Being near bowel or the central biliary tree does not mean giving up ablative intent: tumors <1 cm from luminal GI or central biliary tree go to 60-67.5 Gy in 10-15 fx, with SIB for the 1-2 cm zone. Luminal organ limits, not liver MLD, drive the fractionation choice.
